title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system, and it occurred where a camera alert turns into a police stop. The Flock cameras read letters and numbers only, not plate backgrounds. Kansas issues the same number across more than 100 plate designs, about half of them specialty plates, so a character string that belongs to a stolen vehicle can also be the legitimate number on an unrelated car. The system read what it was built to read, and the match was still wrong.

The failure sits in the handoff from alert to action. In Colwich, officers recognized the vehicle and corrected the entry, which shows a human check can catch the error. In Catoosa, the alert led to a stop with guns drawn and a handcuffing. A Wichita police captain said alerts alone are not enough for a stop, but that officers must act once a stolen tag is confirmed, even when the wrong plate type was entered. Catching this before a stop would have required matching on plate background as well as characters, which the department has discussed training the system to do, or a check of plate type before officers acted, or the state's move to seven digit numbers that are not duplicated.

What is not established is fault. The reporting does not show that the camera software malfunctioned, since it read the characters it was designed to read, and it does not establish that any officer or the company acted improperly. The account rests on a single outlet's investigation.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were repeatedly stopped because their KU Alumni license plate number 7007 matched a stolen GMC pickup's temporary Kansas tag. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police, but officers recognized the vehicle and fixed the entry. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock alert led police to pull them over with guns drawn and handcuff Matthew. The problem is that Kansas duplicates plate numbers across more than 100 designs, about half specialty plates, and Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds.

Wichita police Captain Casey Slaughter said Flock alerts alone are not enough for a stop, but officers must act if a stolen tag is confirmed, even when the wrong plate type was entered. The department has discussed training Flock's AI to recognize plate backgrounds. Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit, non duplicated plate numbers. The Spurlocks' stolen vehicle entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops, and they hope to keep their 14 year old KU tag.
